events.title: Proposed ruling: no_action (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
The rider booked at an upfront quote of $12.71 at 1× surge [F6] and was charged $16.17 at the 1.4× multiplier in effect at trip start [F4][F7]. The whole $3.46 excess is attributable to that multiplier move: the surge element is (1.4 − 1.0) × $10.66 = $4.26, capped by the $3.46 the fare exceeds the quote [F8][SURGE-3]. Nothing in the gap is a route or time overcharge — actual distance 3.9 km equals the optimal 3.9 km (+0.0 km) and the trip ran 5.0 min against a 7.7 min estimate [F1][F2][F3] — so no excess-distance refund arises under the tolerance rule [RD-1][RD-2]. [FARE-0] is satisfied: F5/F7 show base $3.90 + distance $5.46 + time $1.30 + platform $1.25 with the booking fee kept outside the surge.

The notice element is met. The platform log shows the rider was notified in-app at 17:18:45, before the 17:20:00 trip start [F9]. The quoted text states all three SURGE-1 items: the new multiplier ("Fares are 1.4× higher right now"), a revised estimated fare ("Your new estimated fare is $17.29") and a free-cancel option ("You can cancel for free") [F9][SURGE-1]. That the final charge ($16.17) came in below the $17.29 estimate does not make the notice deficient — SURGE-1 requires a stated revised estimate, not a guaranteed final figure [F5][F7][F9]. A rider statement denying notice does not outweigh the platform log, and here the rider's own advocate withdrew the point [F9][F12].

Because the surge rose and the rider was notified and rode, the refund matrix puts the differential on the rider: the higher fare stands [F8][F9][SURGE-2]. The chat contains no route negotiation to disturb this — only a pickup arrangement and the driver's brief reply, both timestamped [F10][F11][F12]; the driver's post-trip statement [F13] adds nothing that changes the fare, which is platform-set [F5][F7][FARE-0].

The rider's single fraud flag ("flagged_for_repeated_fare_disputes", 0 upheld disputes in 90 days) raises the confidence threshold to 95% but never decides the case [F14][TH-3]; the evidence is complete (logged notice, full fare breakdown, complete GPS and timestamped chat), so the threshold is satisfied. The $3.46 in issue is under $10, so the system ruling is final and no human review is required [F8][TH-1][TH-2]. The driver's unrelated dispute history [F15] does not bear on a surge-only fare question. The safety screen found no threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation in the chat, the driver's statement or the complaint [F10][F11][F13].

ruling.recommended_action: Close the dispute with no refund: the $3.46 fare difference was caused solely by the disclosed surge rise and the rider was given compliant pre-trip notice; no driver or rider account action.

The route taken matched the best route and the trip time was within estimate, so nothing points to a fare problem on your side. No action has been taken on your account.

claims.assertion: The rider booked under a binding upfront quote of $12.71 at 1× surge (F6) but was charged $16.17 at 1.4× surge from trip start (F4, F5, F7), so the whole $3.46 excess is attributable to a mid-booking surge increase (F8).

The in-app notice at 17:18:45 (F9) states the multiplier (1.4×), a revised estimated fare ($17.29) and 'You can cancel for free', so on the quoted text alone all three SURGE-1 items appear present and the notice element reads met.
Because the notice states all three items, SURGE-2 gives no_action for the surge differential and the $3.46 surge portion of the claim cannot be recovered.

No part of the fare gap is a route deviation — actual distance 3.9 km equals the optimal 3.9 km (F1, F3) — so no excess-distance refund arises under RD-1/RD-2 and the refund must be measured as the capped surge part: $4.26 uncapped, reduced to the $3.46 by which the fare exceeds the quote (F8).

The rider's fraud flag (1, 'flagged_for_repeated_fare_disputes', F14) is a profile matter only; it raises the confidence threshold to 95% under TH-3 but never decides the case, and the rider has 0 upheld disputes in 90 days (F14).
Amounts under $10 are finally decided by the system, so this $3.46 fare dispute is within the system path regardless of the official document's route-deviation split (TH-1, TH-2, contradiction C1).

weaknesses: The surge notice is fully compliant on its face — F9 quotes all three SURGE-1 items (1.4×, $17.29 revised estimate, free cancellation) — so the rider's 'no notice arrived' grievance loses to the platform log, as the ticket warns, and no_action is the likely ruling on the surge.

The rider carries a fraud flag: F14 shows 1 flag ('flagged_for_repeated_fare_disputes') with 1 dispute in 90 d, which the other side will use to raise the confidence threshold to 95% (TH-3) and to argue credibility against the rider.

The rider's own figures don't match: the complaint asks for $3.46 but the true surge maths in F8 gives $4.26 uncapped, weakening the precision of the claim; and F5/F7 show the fare's other components (base, distance, time, booking fee) are ordinary, leaving little to contest.

claims.assertion: The fare was built up exactly as the policy requires from the trip-start multiplier, so the $16.17 charge is not an overcharge: base $3.90 + distance $5.46 (3.87 km) + time $1.30 (5.0 min) + platform $1.25, with the booking fee of $1.25 kept outside the surge.

The whole $3.46 gap the rider complains about comes from the surge multiplier rising from 1× at quote to 1.4× at trip start: the surge element is (1.4 − 1) × $10.66 = $4.26, capped by the $3.46 the fare exceeds the quote, so no other charge (route, time, waiting) contributes.

The rider was notified in-app at 17:18:45, i.e. before the trip start of 17:20:00, and the logged notice states all three required items: the new multiplier (“Fares are 1.4× higher right now”), the revised estimated fare (“Your new estimated fare is $17.29”) and free cancellation (“You can cancel for free”).
Because the rider was notified of the higher multiplier and rode, the surge-risen fare stands and no part of the differential is refundable.

No route contributor exists to shift the difference onto route grounds: the actual 3.9 km equals the optimal 3.9 km (+0.0 km, −2%) and the trip took 5.0 min against a 7.7 min estimate, so the deviation is nil and RD-1 tolerance is far from being exceeded.

The driver did not set or alter the price and drove the app's route, which is consistent with the GPS record of a zero-excess route and with the fare log that shows no manual adjustment — the only fare increase was the platform surge.

The rider's profile carries 1 fraud flag (flagged_for_repeated_fare_disputes) and 0 upheld disputes in 90 days, which raises the confidence threshold to 95% rather than deciding the case; the fee should still stand because the evidence here is complete and unambiguous.
The amount in issue is $3.46, under $10, so this dispute is finally decided by the system under TH-1/TH-2 and no human review is required.

weaknesses: The notice quotes a revised estimated fare of $17.29 but the rider was finally charged $16.17 (F9 vs F5/F7): the rider will argue the notice was inaccurate, though the policy asks only for a stated estimate, not a guaranteed final figure (SURGE-1).

The rider will deny receiving any notice at all; the only support for notice is the platform surge log F9, which the rider's statement cannot outweigh, but it is a single system record with no separate read receipt or acknowledgement.
The rider's $12.71 quote (F6) is a real upfront quote and the rider has already been charged $3.46 above it (F8), so the judge starts from a visible price increase the rider did not ask for.

The driver has 2 upheld disputes in 90 days (F15) while route and no-show counts are 0; the rider may use this history to argue the driver is dispute-prone, even though those upheld matters are unrelated to surge pricing.

points.response: Conceded on the arithmetic: the components in F5/F7 (base $3.90, distance $5.46, time $1.30, platform $1.25 at cost) are computed per FARE-0, so the charge is a correct application of the higher trip-start multiplier — the only live question is whether that $3.46 gap is refundable under SURGE-2.

Conceded: the entire $3.46 gap is the surge move from 1× to 1.4× (F6, F7, F8), with the surge element capped at $3.46 and no route or time component mixed in (F1, F2), so nothing in the difference can be shifted to RD-2.

Conceded on the quoted text: F9 is logged before trip start at 17:18:45 and its words contain all three SURGE-1 items (1.4×, a $17.29 revised estimate, 'You can cancel for free'), so I do not contest that the element reads met.
Conceded: because the notice is logged and complete (F9), SURGE-2's 'rider notified → no_action' row applies and the $3.46 surge differential is not refundable.

No contest — F1 and F3 both show actual 3.9 km against optimal 3.9 km (+0.0 km), so no RD-1 tolerance breach and no RD-2 excess-distance refund arises; this claim's outcome turns entirely on the surge clause.

Conceded so far as it goes: F1 shows zero excess distance and F5 shows no manual adjustment, and the driver's statement in F13 that 'I don't set the price; the app does' is not contradicted by any system record, so the driver personally pocketed no route or price excess.

I accept the flag raises the threshold to 95% under TH-3 and does not decide the case; but the rider's 0 upheld disputes in 90 days (F14) and, per F15, the driver's 2 upheld disputes in 90 days cut the other way on credibility, so the driver's claim on credibility is not one-sided.
Conceded: $3.46 is under $10, so TH-1/TH-2 make the system ruling final and no human review is needed.

Withdrawing my C2/C3 push for a refund: on the words of F9 the notice element is met and SURGE-2 yields no_action, so I no longer ask for the $3.46; my brief's C1/C4 findings on the $3.46 ceiling remain true on the record but support no refund.

The $3.46 gap does indeed arise from the multiplier rising to 1.4× at trip start (F8, F4), but C1's own facts then defeat the claim: the ride began after the logged 17:18:45 notice (F9), so the quote ceased to be the binding price once the rider was told of the new multiplier and rode anyway (SURGE-1, SURGE-2).
Agreed on the reading of the text: I share it and I read SURGE-1:notice as met, the notice stating the 1.4× multiplier, the $17.29 revised estimate and free cancellation (F9).
Conceded: on that notice the surge-risen fare stands and the $3.46 cannot be recovered (F8, F9).

Conceded: the route contributed nothing — 3.9 km actual against 3.9 km optimal (F1, F3) — so no RD-1/RD-2 excess-distance refund arises and the only figure in play is the capped surge part of $3.46 (F8).

Agreed the flag never decides the case; it only lifts the threshold to 95% (F14), which is met here because the records are complete (timestamped chat F12, logged notice F9), one rule row applies, and the trip's own GPS shows zero excess distance (F1).
No dispute: at $3.46 the matter is under $10 and finally decided by the system (F8), so the ruling should issue without human review.

I withdraw nothing, but I narrow D6: the driver statement (F13) is not needed to prove the price was platform-set — the fare build-up in F5/F7 shows the only variable above the quote was the surge multiplier, and the phone chat shows no in-trip negotiation (F10, F11).

The higher fare came from a rise in the surge multiplier between booking and trip start, and the rider was sent an in-app notice about it, including a revised estimate and a free-cancel option, before the trip began.
